concepts.name: virtual reality
concepts.definition: Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.

defining_facts.text: Virtual reality (VR) is, according to the Miriam Webster dictionary, an artificial environment experienced through sensory stimuli, in which sights and sounds play a primary role and are provided by a computer, possibly along with other sensory stimuli, and in which a person's actions partially determine what happens in the environment.
Augmented reality (AR) alters the ongoing perception of the real world, whereas virtual reality (VR) completely replaces the user's sense of reality with a virtual environment.

A virtual reality (VR) system does not require the physical existence of an object or place, because it creates a virtual environment, whereas an augmented reality (AR) or mixed reality (MR) system requires the place being experienced to exist.

The early era in the historical evolution of virtual reality (VR) is the period before modern digital computers were developed in the 1940s, and although not everything was present in that era, a few key developments were conceptually similar to immersive virtual reality experiences.

In virtual reality (VR), headsets or display devices present two-dimensional (2D) images, but stereoscopic vision makes the user perceive them as three-dimensional (3D) objects and space, which is immersion.

The flight simulator concept introduced for the first time in 1928 by Edwin A. Link evolved into sophisticated flight simulators with multiple sensors that provide an immersive experience, and this early development is considered a precursor to modern multi-sensory immersive virtual reality (VR).

The main objective of any virtual reality (VR) system is to let the user experience an artificial environment through sensory stimuli provided by the computer, not only for sight and sound but for all sensory organs.

There are broadly two major issues in experiencing virtual reality (VR): the technological issue of how to generate suitable sensory stimuli for the artificial environment, and the psychological issue of how to perceive those stimuli suitably, a human-factor issue that technology does not address and that is likely to differ between users.

The technological and psychological issues in virtual reality (VR) give rise to two major concerns that appear in almost every literature on VR technology or experience, namely immersion and presence.
The causes of cyber sickness are broadly internal factors and external factors, and external factors comprise hardware and virtual reality (VR) content.

Cyber sickness can be independent of age when users view general virtual reality (VR) content, while age may be a factor for controllable content, making the age relationship clearer for controllable content.

A possible reason for increased cyber sickness among female head-mounted display (HMD) users is inter-pupillary distance (IPD) fit, because IPD determines stereoscopic vision and a greater proportion of females may have trouble finding a good fit; this implies virtual reality (VR) displays should have a wider IPD adjustable range for female users.

Virtual reality (VR) recreates realistic movement and visual environments, making the user feel as if in a real-world environment; therefore, users with motion sickness (MS) susceptibility tend also to have cyber sickness susceptibility.

Prior exposure to virtual reality (VR) systems and repeated exposure to VR can reduce the effect of motion sickness (MS) susceptibility on cyber sickness and reduce cyber sickness severity over time, so the positive correlation may not hold if either or both conditions are satisfied.

A user's physical position affects cyber sickness susceptibility: using a virtual reality (VR) system in a standing posture is likely to induce more cyber sickness, or more severe cyber sickness, than using the same system while sitting.

A virtual reality (VR) system is designed to create interactions that make the user feel immersed, and the amount of presence and the quality of the overall experience depend on fooling the user's perceptual system into believing the virtual system is the familiar real world.
Virtual reality generally provides the brain with sensory signals that are inconsistent with the user's real-life experiences and behavior.

One possible outcome of generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation is that the body adapts to the new stimuli, making the user unaware of any flaws in the system and causing the user to believe that the virtual system is the real world rather than an artificial system.

Another possible outcome of generally inconsistent virtual reality stimulation is that the body may not be able to adapt, causing increased fatigue or headaches, and this non-adaptation may lead to cyber sickness, that is, dizziness, nausea, or a large set of different symptoms experienced while using virtual reality systems.
An understanding of human perception is needed to design a better virtual reality (VR) system or to identify and resolve flaws in a given system.

In the Unity editor interface, the preference tab lets the developer select extended reality (XR) settings for three system types: virtual reality, which simulates a completely artificial environment around the user; mixed reality, which combines Unity's own environment with the user's real world environment and allows the environments to interact; and augmented reality, which provides layers of content over a digital view of the real world.

concepts.name: head-mounted display
concepts.definition: The formative years of virtual reality are the second phase of its historical evolution, roughly 1950 to 1990 after computers appeared in the 1940s, beginning with development of head-mounted displays (HMDs) in the 1950s and ending with popularization of the term virtual reality in the late 1980s.

defining_facts.text: The formative years of virtual reality are the second phase of its historical evolution, roughly 1950 to 1990 after computers appeared in the 1940s, beginning with development of head-mounted displays (HMDs) in the 1950s and ending with popularization of the term virtual reality in the late 1980s.

In the 1950s, especially toward the latter half of the decade, people started working on and considering different types of head-mounted displays (HMDs), a new kind of computer display that was less common than regular computer monitors.
In 1961, engineers at Philco Corporation developed an early head-mounted display (HMD) that could track users' motion but was bulky and uncomfortable to wear.
In 1965, Tom Furness and colleagues at the Wright-Patterson Air Force Base worked on visually coupled systems for pilots that consisted of head-mounted displays (HMDs).
In 1967, Sutherland developed the Sword of Damocles, a head-mounted display (HMD), and was the first to demonstrate an HMD with head tracking and computer-generated imagery.

In 1985, Scott Fisher and colleagues at the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) developed and launched Virtual Visual Environment Display (VIVED), the first commercially viable and commercially available stereoscopic head-tracked head-mounted display (HMD) with a wide field of view.

The three broad types of visual displays are head-mounted displays (HMDs), which are wearable and mobile, world-fixed displays, which are not wearable and are stationary, and regular displays, which are mobile or can be stationary.
Although head-mounted displays (HMDs) can be used as input to track head motion, their primary use is as a display device.
A head-mounted display (HMD) is a sophisticated piece of equipment that integrates electronic, optical, mechanical, and audio components within its package.

A head-mounted display (HMD) places images directly in front of the user's eyes using one or two small screens, with one screen providing monoscopic viewing and two screens providing stereoscopic viewing, and stereoscopic HMDs are more common than monoscopic HMDs.
Head-mounted displays (HMDs) can be further categorized into three types: non-see-through, optical see-through, and video see-through.

Non-see-through HMDs are typically used in virtual reality (VR), optical see-through HMDs are typically used in augmented reality (AR), and video see-through HMDs are typically used in augmented virtuality, in which real-world images or videos appear in real time within an artificial or virtual environment.

concepts.name: virtual reality system
concepts.definition: A virtual reality (VR) system is defined by three characteristics: an artificial or synthetic environment, sensory experience through computer-generated stimuli, and user actions that partially determine what happens in the environment; a system with these aspects can be categorized as a virtual reality system and distinguished from other systems, which are not supposed to have these aspects.

defining_facts.text: A virtual reality (VR) system is defined by three characteristics: an artificial or synthetic environment, sensory experience through computer-generated stimuli, and user actions that partially determine what happens in the environment; a system with these aspects can be categorized as a virtual reality system and distinguished from other systems, which are not supposed to have these aspects.

The artificial or synthetic environment of a virtual reality (VR) system is a computer-generated graphical representation of a real world or an imaginary or fantastic world, populated with artificial objects, and is not a real environment.

An artificial environment in a virtual reality (VR) system can recreate a real world using real-world imagery or video, as in a virtual tour, but it still counts as a virtual reality system because it is a computer-generated scenario and changes are not happening in real time.

The sensory experience characteristic of a virtual reality (VR) system means that the system provides computer-generated stimuli to the user's sensory organs, such as eyes and ears, so the user can immersively experience the artificial or synthetic environment, and this immersive experience is a hallmark of a virtual reality system.

The user interaction characteristic of a virtual reality (VR) system means that the system must be interactive: the user can act on or interact with elements in the environment, and user actions or inputs partially determine what happens in the environment, producing dynamic changes in the virtual environment, just as people interact with objects in the real world.

A system is a virtual reality (VR) system if it satisfies all three characteristics of a VR system—virtual environment, immersive experience through sensory organs, and interaction—and it is not a VR system if it does not satisfy at least one of them.

A computer-aided design (CAD) system is not a virtual reality (VR) system because, although it supports a virtual environment and interaction, it does not support an immersive experience, since the user interacts with screen content through a mouse while still seeing the real world around the computer screen.

A video conferencing system is not a virtual reality (VR) system because, although it is interactive, it is not a virtual environment or an immersive experience, since it presents a real-world environment in real time through a screen and the user remains in the real world, with the screen only aiding interaction.

A three-dimensional (3D) movie experience is not a virtual reality (VR) system because, although it provides a virtual environment and a partly immersive experience, it is not interactive, as the viewer only watches and cannot change the displayed content.
A complete view of a virtual reality (VR) system consists of the organism, the VR hardware, and the surrounding physical world.

In the complete view of a virtual reality (VR) system, data flow from the organism to the VR hardware is labeled tracking, data flow from the VR hardware to the organism is labeled stimulation, and bidirectional data flows exist between the VR hardware and the surrounding physical world and between the surrounding physical world and the organism.

In a complete view of a virtual reality (VR) system, the organism component, which typically refers to the human user, is equally important to account for as the VR hardware component and cannot be omitted because the user is always present.
The overall virtual reality (VR) system has three components: the user, the hardware, and the surrounding physical environment.

The surrounding physical environment is considered part of the virtual reality (VR) system because the user may respond to real-world stimuli such as light, sound, and smell, and may not be completely detached from the real world, so the environment may affect the user's behavior while interacting with the virtual world.

concepts.name: presence
concepts.definition: Presence is the psychological side that captures whether a user perceives the immersive qualities that are generated.

defining_facts.text: Presence is the psychological side that captures whether a user perceives the immersive qualities that are generated.

Presence is defined by the International Society for Presence Research, which has had the definition since 2000, as a psychological state or subjective perception in which part or all of an individual's current experience is generated by or filtered through human-made technology, but part or all of the individual's perception fails to accurately acknowledge the role of the technology in the experience.

Presence is a state in which computer-generated stimuli stimulate the user's sensory organs, and the user's perception is as good as perceiving reality because the user cannot distinguish those stimuli from real-world stimuli, so the user perceives them as coming from the real world rather than from a computer.

Presence is a state of consciousness or psychological sense of being in the virtual environment that exists inside the user's mind, has no direct manifestation, is difficult to measure objectively, and therefore requires the user's subjective experience to be taken into account.

Presence can be a function of both the user's subjective experience and a system's immersion, that is the objective or technological experience, so immersion can aid an enhanced perception of presence and is capable of producing presence, but it does not ensure presence.

Presence can be limited by immersion, and the greater the immersion a system or application provides, the greater the potential for a user to feel present in the virtual world, while the lesser the immersive technology provides, the lesser the presence.

The overall goal of any virtual reality system is to create a high degree of presence, that is to make users feel that they are really in the virtual world and unable to distinguish the real world from the virtual world.
Creating a high degree of presence in a virtual reality system requires the system to provide a high degree of immersion, and this requirement is a systemic issue.

The goal of any virtual reality (VR) system is to create a high degree of presence, meaning that people believe they are in the real world while they are actually in a virtual world, and the closer a VR system is to this goal, the better the immersive experience it provides.

Cybersickness (CS) mitigation involves a trade-off between reducing cybersickness and preserving user experience, because mitigation strategies often affect presence or the user's ability to perceive the virtual world, and presence affects user experience.

Mark Weiser's quote that the most profound technologies are those that disappear and presence refer to the same thing: the technological aspect surrounding the user should disappear from the user's perception, and the goal is to build systems that do not make it apparent that the user is using a specialized technological product.

In an Extended Reality (XR) system, the interaction and the perceptual stimuli, the latter being the output generated by the system, are designed to create the best possible illusion of reality, not actual reality, in order to enhance presence, which is a sense of reality as if the user is in the real world.

Presence in a virtual environment requires both reinforcing the virtual experience as believable and developing attachment to that experience, and the auditory experience plays a very important role in increasing presence in the virtual environment.

The key concerns to be addressed in the Majuli Island virtual reality (VR) Tour are capturing both the tangible and intangible aspects of the island's cultural heritage, which is the broader objective, the user experience, specifically the extent to which users feel present in the virtual island, and minimizing the risk of cyber sickness while users explore the island.
Presence is a psychological state of mind that is measured by standard questionnaires.
The QEP questionnaire was used to measure presence, and it is a 2004 revised version of the standard presence questionnaire (PQ).

The presence measure used to evaluate the virtual tour of Majuli Island included involvement, interface quality, adaptation or immersion, and visual fidelity, and tangible and intangible reconstruction fidelity was additionally reported for participants who had previously visited Majuli Island.

The overall user presence ratings for the virtual tour of Majuli Island were involvement mean 5.65 (standard deviation 1.11, coefficient of variation 0.19), interface quality mean 4.37 (standard deviation 1.4, coefficient of variation 0.32), adaptation and immersion mean 5.4 (standard deviation 1.13, coefficient of variation 0.2), and visual fidelity mean 5.79 (standard deviation 0.93, coefficient of variation 0.16).

The presence ratings for participants who had previously visited Majuli Island were tangible and intangible reconstruction fidelity mean 5.68 (standard deviation 1, coefficient of variation 0.177), involvement mean 5.83 (standard deviation 1.05, coefficient of variation 0.18), interface quality mean 4.72 (standard deviation 1.36, coefficient of variation 0.33), adaptation or immersion mean 5.61 (standard deviation 1.15, coefficient of variation 0.22), and visual fidelity mean 5.94 (standard deviation 0.93, coefficient of variation 0.15).

The overall presence results for the virtual tour of Majuli Island were summarized as good presence, meaning that users felt reasonably well located within the virtual environment while virtually exploring Majuli Island.

never_defined.name: headset
never_defined.definition: To different people, hearing extended reality (XR), virtual reality (VR), augmented reality (AR), or mixed reality (MR) may lead them to associate one or more of these terms with magical movie scenes such as those in Avatar, interactive video games, 3D or 4D movie-theater documentaries about extinct animals, a user wearing a headset that blocks vision and transports the user to a virtual world, which is the most common perception of VR, games such as Pokémon Go in which the real world is visible on a device screen and virtual objects that do not exist in the real world can also be seen on that screen, or visualizations of internal body structures such as a skeleton or veins.

never_defined.name: virtual world
never_defined.definition: To different people, hearing extended reality (XR), virtual reality (VR), augmented reality (AR), or mixed reality (MR) may lead them to associate one or more of these terms with magical movie scenes such as those in Avatar, interactive video games, 3D or 4D movie-theater documentaries about extinct animals, a user wearing a headset that blocks vision and transports the user to a virtual world, which is the most common perception of VR, games such as Pokémon Go in which the real world is visible on a device screen and virtual objects that do not exist in the real world can also be seen on that screen, or visualizations of internal body structures such as a skeleton or veins.

never_defined.name: reference frame
never_defined.definition: Location-based markerless augmented reality (AR) applications rely on a location sensor, such as a global positioning system (GPS) sensor, to detect the user's location with respect to a reference frame, and digital content is augmented on the real-world view when the user is at a specific location.

never_defined.name: computer vision
never_defined.definition: Markerless augmented reality (AR) techniques rely primarily on computer vision and may rely on other sensors, such as global positioning system (GPS) sensors, in location-based applications.

never_defined.name: three-dimensional space
never_defined.definition: In virtual reality (VR), headsets or display devices present two-dimensional (2D) images, but stereoscopic vision makes the user perceive them as three-dimensional (3D) objects and space, which is immersion.

never_defined.name: head tracking
never_defined.definition: In 1967, Sutherland developed the Sword of Damocles, a head-mounted display (HMD), and was the first to demonstrate an HMD with head tracking and computer-generated imagery.

never_defined.name: data glove
never_defined.definition: In 1987, two papers appeared in Scientific American, one on the data glove, an input device, and these papers helped shape and popularize the field of virtual reality.

never_defined.name: smartphone
never_defined.definition: In 2004, the first mobile-phone based augmented reality (AR) application was demonstrated and the AR Toolkit was ported to mobile phones, and although early mobile phones looked different from modern-day smartphones, people still tried to use early mobile phones to develop mobile-based augmented reality applications.

never_defined.name: fatigue
never_defined.definition: A large number of symptoms may indicate the onset of cybersickness (CS) or cybersickness itself, and common ones include nausea, headache, excessive sweating, dryness of mouth, fullness of stomach, vomiting or a tendency to vomit, dizziness, disorientation, fatigue, and strange hand-eye coordination in which coordination does not happen in the expected way, so if one or more of these symptoms occur during a virtual reality (VR) experience, cybersickness can be assumed to be happening or going to happen.

never_defined.name: joystick
never_defined.definition: In virtual reality (VR), motion controllers such as steering with handlebars may cause more cybersickness (CS) than non-motion controls such as a joystick, and a gamepad controller causes less cybersickness than a hand controller.

never_defined.name: head movement
never_defined.definition: An excessively narrow field of view (FOV) in virtual reality (VR) can decrease immersion and increase head movement to look for things in the environment, which may exacerbate or increase cybersickness (CS); finding the optimal FOV is crucial for creating a comfortable VR experience.

never_defined.name: data flow
never_defined.definition: In the complete view of a virtual reality (VR) system, data flow from the organism to the VR hardware is labeled tracking, data flow from the VR hardware to the organism is labeled stimulation, and bidirectional data flows exist between the VR hardware and the surrounding physical world and between the surrounding physical world and the organism.

never_defined.name: stimulus
never_defined.definition: In a virtual reality (VR) system, the data flow between the hardware and the user (organism) is bidirectional: stimulation data flow carries hardware-generated stimuli that override the user's senses, and tracking data flow uses sensors to track user motions so the hardware can adjust the stimuli based on those motions.

never_defined.name: user motion
never_defined.definition: In a virtual reality (VR) system, the data flow between the hardware and the user (organism) is bidirectional: stimulation data flow carries hardware-generated stimuli that override the user's senses, and tracking data flow uses sensors to track user motions so the hardware can adjust the stimuli based on those motions.

never_defined.name: button press
never_defined.definition: In a virtual reality (VR) system, head tracking is commonly used and is the most important thing to track, while tracking may also include button presses (including which button is pressed in which context), controller movements, eye movements, and movements of other body parts.

never_defined.name: controller movement
never_defined.definition: In a virtual reality (VR) system, head tracking is commonly used and is the most important thing to track, while tracking may also include button presses (including which button is pressed in which context), controller movements, eye movements, and movements of other body parts.

never_defined.name: eye movement
never_defined.definition: In a virtual reality (VR) system, head tracking is commonly used and is the most important thing to track, while tracking may also include button presses (including which button is pressed in which context), controller movements, eye movements, and movements of other body parts.

never_defined.name: body part movement
never_defined.definition: In a virtual reality (VR) system, head tracking is commonly used and is the most important thing to track, while tracking may also include button presses (including which button is pressed in which context), controller movements, eye movements, and movements of other body parts.

never_defined.name: surrounding physical environment
never_defined.definition: The overall virtual reality (VR) system has three components: the user, the hardware, and the surrounding physical environment.

never_defined.name: tracker
never_defined.definition: Virtual reality (VR) hardware may include trackers that track objects in the surrounding physical environment rather than the user directly, and this is required especially when interaction with those objects is part of the experience.

never_defined.name: immersive application
never_defined.definition: Virtual reality (VR) hardware may change the surrounding physical environment, for example when an immersive application uses a robotic arm to change the position of objects in the environment, and that change may affect the user's behavior.

never_defined.name: robotic arm
never_defined.definition: Virtual reality (VR) hardware may change the surrounding physical environment, for example when an immersive application uses a robotic arm to change the position of objects in the environment, and that change may affect the user's behavior.

never_defined.name: controller
never_defined.definition: Virtual reality (VR) hardware is not limited to only the computer, head-mounted display (HMD), or controller used by the user; it may deal with objects in the surrounding physical environment.

never_defined.name: tracking device
never_defined.definition: In virtual reality (VR) hardware, a sensor or input device is used in a broad sense to mean any tracking device that tracks the user's input and extracts information from the real world, with the discussion restricted to sensors that track the user's movements.

never_defined.name: virtual reality input device
never_defined.definition: Virtual reality (VR) input devices are broadly divided into hand input devices, which require hands to operate, and non-hand input devices, which do not require hands to operate.

never_defined.name: portability
never_defined.definition: World-grounded hand input devices are devices that are fixed in the real world and do not move; a joystick is an example that is commonly used to interact with desktop or other grounded systems, and portability is an issue because they constrain the user to move within a specified area.

never_defined.name: button
never_defined.definition: Non-tracked handheld controllers are hand input devices that are held in the hand but are not tracked in three-dimensional (3D) space, so the system does not know their exact position with respect to a reference frame; examples include buttons, joysticks, triggers, and traditional video game controllers.

never_defined.name: traditional video game controller
never_defined.definition: Non-tracked handheld controllers are hand input devices that are held in the hand but are not tracked in three-dimensional (3D) space, so the system does not know their exact position with respect to a reference frame; examples include buttons, joysticks, triggers, and traditional video game controllers.

never_defined.name: break-in presence
never_defined.definition: Non-tracked handheld controllers can cause break-in presence because the user's untracked hand movements may not produce a corresponding change in the position of the virtual hands in the virtual world, creating discomfort about whether the user is performing the task appropriately and affecting the perception of presence in the virtual world.

never_defined.name: six degrees of freedom tracking
never_defined.definition: Tracked handheld controllers are hand input devices with six degrees of freedom tracking, so the system can track their movements; input controllers that come with modern virtual reality (VR) systems are tracked devices so that break-in presence is avoided, and VIVE controllers are an example because they combine a joystick with tracking and are mainly used in VR.

never_defined.name: VIVE controller
never_defined.definition: Tracked handheld controllers are hand input devices with six degrees of freedom tracking, so the system can track their movements; input controllers that come with modern virtual reality (VR) systems are tracked devices so that break-in presence is avoided, and VIVE controllers are an example because they combine a joystick with tracking and are mainly used in VR.

never_defined.name: force feedback controller
never_defined.definition: Tracked handheld controllers have the limitation that users cannot directly or fully touch and feel passive virtual objects through tangible interaction because the user's hands are occupied with the controller, although force feedback controllers may sometimes resolve the issue.

never_defined.name: tangible interaction
never_defined.definition: Tracked handheld controllers have the limitation that users cannot directly or fully touch and feel passive virtual objects through tangible interaction because the user's hands are occupied with the controller, although force feedback controllers may sometimes resolve the issue.

never_defined.name: passive virtual object
never_defined.definition: Tracked handheld controllers have the limitation that users cannot directly or fully touch and feel passive virtual objects through tangible interaction because the user's hands are occupied with the controller, although force feedback controllers may sometimes resolve the issue.

never_defined.name: electromyography band
never_defined.definition: Hand-worn hand input devices are devices that are worn on the hands, arms, or fingers; examples include data gloves, electromyography (EMG) bands, and rings, with data gloves being more popular.

never_defined.name: ring
never_defined.definition: Hand-worn hand input devices are devices that are worn on the hands, arms, or fingers; examples include data gloves, electromyography (EMG) bands, and rings, with data gloves being more popular.

never_defined.name: bend sensor
never_defined.definition: Bend-sensing data gloves are data gloves with sensors at all bend positions or joints and other positions; their processing unit receives continuous raw data from these bend sensors and processes it to detect hand postures and gestures, and because their many sensors make any gesture likely to generate a different data stream for unambiguous interpretation, they provide a large degree of freedom that can make interaction more natural than controller-based interaction.

never_defined.definition: Bend-sensing data gloves are data gloves with sensors at all bend positions or joints and other positions; their processing unit receives continuous raw data from these bend sensors and processes it to detect hand postures and gestures, and because their many sensors make any gesture likely to generate a different data stream for unambiguous interpretation, they provide a large degree of freedom that can make interaction more natural than controller-based interaction.

never_defined.definition: Bend-sensing data gloves are data gloves with sensors at all bend positions or joints and other positions; their processing unit receives continuous raw data from these bend sensors and processes it to detect hand postures and gestures, and because their many sensors make any gesture likely to generate a different data stream for unambiguous interpretation, they provide a large degree of freedom that can make interaction more natural than controller-based interaction.

never_defined.name: pinch gesture
never_defined.definition: Pinch gloves are data gloves in which the sensors are placed only at fingertip positions, which may vary but often include the thumb and index finger fingertips; they detect a limited set of pinch gestures, are good at determining whether the fingertips are touching, and are typically used for discrete input such as object selection and mode switching.

never_defined.definition: Pinch gloves are data gloves in which the sensors are placed only at fingertip positions, which may vary but often include the thumb and index finger fingertips; they detect a limited set of pinch gestures, are good at determining whether the fingertips are touching, and are typically used for discrete input such as object selection and mode switching.

never_defined.name: line-of-sight issue
never_defined.definition: The advantages of hand-worn hand input devices are natural input with potentially rich gesture interaction, comfortable hand positions, no line-of-sight issue unlike some controller-based input, and the ability of the user's hands and fingers to fully interact with real objects, making different sorts of perception possible.

never_defined.name: infrared
never_defined.definition: The Leap Motion device is an example of a bare-hand input device: it is an infrared (IR)-based hand-tracking sensor that typically contains three IR light-emitting diodes (LEDs) and two wide-angle cameras; the LEDs generate IR light reflected from the hands and picked up by the cameras, and software converts the signals into gestures.

never_defined.definition: The Leap Motion device can be attached to a head-mounted display (HMD) to provide hand input support even if the HMD does not support hand input, and it is typically useful with low-cost HMDs that do not provide good-quality controllers or controller support, such as cardboard-type devices in which a smartphone provides a stereoscopic view and which do not support interaction.
